title: Best LLM to be a brainstorming partner?
author: rapkannibale
selftext: Wondering what people's experience are that have tried different LLMs to be their game design brainstorming partner? Which one is the most creative and actually contributes ideas and pushes back on things that you propose that might not work, etc? Thanks!

comments.author: Troph_A
comments.body: Don't know which is the best, but chatgpt is the worst.

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body: ask for adversial reviews, most llms have harnesses that push for helpfulness. you need to specifially ask it to give you a hard time. and putting it custom instructions doesn't work alot, you need to be specific in the prompts

comments.author: Binoui
comments.body:
Agentic work is not just about model choice, it's about setting up an environment that matches your needs. I recommend working locally and setting up a project with brainstorming skills and key documentation files. As you're building the project, make a point to document regularly so following agents can have the right context to help you think.

Here's my personal project's docs as reference, not perfect but I've been happy with how it's been developing and correct AI has been crucial. https://github.com/Binoui/SlopArena/tree/main/docs

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
IMO, the problem with brainstorming in general is that

1. It’s better to brainstorm without a partner,

1. LLMs don’t understand how humans respond to your ideas or evaluate whether something you say makes logical sense. 

I use LLMs for programming, documentation, and gathering research materials.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
I mean, that happens all the time with people too.  There's some colossally bad ideas for projects that get yes-manned or have a creator too busy sniffing their own farts to admit its flaws.

Having a different perspective to bounce ideas off of and do research with is a very powerful thing for brainstorming.  When I'm working out a game system, being able to ask "how did it work in XYZ game?" and having the tool do that research in seconds for me to reference is extremely helpful.  Like with anything its all in how you use it - don't cede full creative control to an LLM

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: The LLM doesn’t have a perspective, though. It is just a tool for generating text.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body: The LLM doesn’t have a perspective, though. It is just a tool for generating text.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
What do you mean it "doesn't have a perspective?"  Sure it does, it has the aggregated perspective of discourse surrounding similar game systems from its training data.  It's perspective is pretty much an accurate mean perspective of whatever the topic is across the sample of discussion of that topic.

That's *extremely* valuable for bouncing ideas off of.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
It doesn’t have an aggregated perspective. It has a statistical model of what textual responses are. 

Seriously.

LLMs in general do not play games and don’t model what it’s like to play games. That’s simply not part of their architecture.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
Yes, I know how they work technically.

If that's the rationale you want to take, then people are just a biological model of electrons firing through synapses in a brain, and they don't know "what it's like to play games" either, and we get to go down the rabbit hole of "what defines the human condition? Is there a soul? But that's not constructive or topical.

I think the real issue is that you're misunderstanding what brainstorming is for and confusing it with gathering user feedback via playtesting.  AI cannot specifically gather "look and feel" playtesting feedback for exactly the reasons you describe, but that has nothing to do with brainstorming and ideation during design.  When you tell an AI "I'm thinking of doing XYZ game mechanic" and it responds with "that clashes with your other system ABC and players typically don't like that," that's valuable and stops exactly the scenarios that OP is talking about - sunk dev time in a poorly formed mechanic.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
People aren’t a “biological model of electrons” in any way other than some weird technical sense

Humans know what it’s like to play games because we actually play games and have those experiences. This is pretty obvious stuff and I can’t imagine why you’re arguing against that, unless maybe you just like arguing.

AI is a bad partner for brainstorming, that’s all.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
>People aren’t a “biological model of electrons” in any way other than some weird technical sense

Correct, that's literally the point I was making, I was being intentionally reductive to illustrate how you're looking at this whole thing in some "weird technical sense" while ignoring what the models actually *do*.

>Humans know what it’s like to play games because we actually play games and have those experiences. This is pretty obvious stuff and I can’t imagine why you’re arguing against that, unless maybe you just like arguing.

You're doing that unnecessary philosophizing that I pointed out here.  And if I "just liked arguing" I would have latched on to your initial statement of "it's better to brainstorm without a partner" which is complete and total nonsense in the objective sense.

>AI is a bad partner for brainstorming, that’s all.

It's really not, that's all.

comments.author: NotYourValidation
comments.body:
Partner? None. For an LLM to run ideas by from a technical and logical point of view? Probably Claude.  
  
For the best experience, learn at least the fundamentals of Game Design first and then only use LLM to complement your design progress. Specifically talking about game design here, you as the human are the most creative. It requires a human to discover what is fun, what works, what doesn't work, what's engaging and what isn't. An LLM is terrible at doing that stuff. It's great with organizing everything once you lock down the core game design, and maybe it can offer advice on what you've come up with, but it can never know how it *feels* to play a game (like when we use a bug as a feature because it makes the game more fun), so it will never really know the right time to push back or to greenlight something.

Just have a quick look at all the low effort AI trash games out there. They all suffer from the same problem. Someone let AI take the wheel on game design (or partnered on it), and it turned out to be a big steaming pile of shit. With game design, you do the legwork, and then AI assist you when you get stuck on something or need a logical perspective because that's all it's really good for.

As another commenter pointed out, use a prompt that will force the LLM to be your logic checker not your game design friend.

"Act as a cynical, highly analytical systems designer. I am going to give you the core loop of my game. Do not praise it. Do not add narrative flavor. Your only job is to look at the mechanics and tell me where the system will grind to a halt, where players will find game-breaking exploits, and what mechanics are fundamentally fighting against each other."

comments.author: ididmr2
comments.body:
I think Claude- Sonnet. Opus is horrific- so verbose to say nothing. 

But genuinely play around with asking it for feedback on something you know is wrong, from a human perspective- or at least where your taste dictates it's the wrong direction. Rephrase and see how much it gasses you up and encourages you down whatever direction. 

These games are supposed to be played by humans, you genuinely need human feedback. There's a reason musical artists lose their ability once they're surrounded by yes men. It's going to be the same with an LLM. It provides the illusion of feedback.
